Timeline::concat¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signatures¶

Timeline Timeline::concat(const Timeline& other) const
Timeline Timeline::concat(const std::vector<Timeline>& others) const

Assemble Records Along Axis Zero¶

concat() constructs one Timeline by placing complete temporal blocks one after another along axis 0. It is structural assembly: values are not sorted, parsed again, compared, or made distinct. Every stored instant, including NaT, keeps its position inside its source block.

Use the single-value overload when appending one block. Use the vector overload when the complete sequence of blocks is already available; it validates the whole sequence and allocates the destination once, avoiding a chain of increasingly large intermediate timelines.

Shape Contract¶

For non-scalar inputs, every operand must have the same rank and the same dimensions after axis 0. If A has shape [a, d1, ..., dn] and B has shape [b, d1, ..., dn], their result has shape [a + b, d1, ..., dn].

This makes each axis-0 slice a record whose trailing shape is fixed. A [2, 3] block can join a [5, 3] block, but not a [5, 2] block and not a rank-one [3] vector.

Scalars are the deliberate exception. Each scalar is promoted to a one-element sequence, so scalar plus scalar produces shape [2]. Scalar promotion does not make a scalar compatible with a matrix: after promotion their ranks still differ.

Receiver

scalar

Example 1. Joining two one-row matrices retains the column axis; it does not flatten the four instants into shape [4].

const auto jan12 = pluss::timeline::date({{"2024-01-01", "2024-01-02"}});
const auto jan34 = pluss::timeline::date({{"2024-01-03", "2024-01-04"}});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(jan12.concat(jan34)) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2, 2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]
[ 2024-01-03 00:00:00 2024-01-04 00:00:00 ]

Joining Several Blocks¶

The vector overload treats others in iteration order. The receiver is always first, followed by others[0], others[1], and so on. Passing an empty vector is valid and returns the receiver’s values and shape in fresh contiguous storage.

Example 2. Three one-row matrices become a three-row matrix in call order.

const auto jan56 = pluss::timeline::date({{"2024-01-05", "2024-01-06"}});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(jan12.concat({jan34, jan56})) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[3, 2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]
[ 2024-01-03 00:00:00 2024-01-04 00:00:00 ]
[ 2024-01-05 00:00:00 2024-01-06 00:00:00 ]

Example 3. Scalar promotion and an explicitly empty block list are separate call forms.

const auto joined_scalars = pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-01")
                                .concat(pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-02"));
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(joined_scalars) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(
    jan12.concat(std::vector<pluss::Timeline>{})) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]
Timeline(shape=[1, 2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:00:00 ]

Timezone And Storage Rules¶

All operands must carry the same timezone name. concat() does not silently choose one display calendar, even when differently labelled timelines contain the same UTC instants. Convert deliberately with tz_convert() before joining. The result keeps the receiver’s timezone.

Inputs may be contiguous or strided. Values are copied in logical index order, not raw allocation order, and the result is newly allocated contiguous storage. The operation is linear in the total number of copied instants and requires storage for exactly that total.

Example 4. A stride-two view contributes its logical dates, not the padding values between them.

std::array<std::int64_t, 4> backing{
    1'704'067'200'000'000'000LL, 11,
    1'704'153'600'000'000'000LL, 22};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> shape{2};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{2};
const auto strided = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
    backing.data(), shape, strides, {}, "UTC");
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(
    strided.concat(pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-03"))) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[3], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-02 00:00:00, 2024-01-03 00:00:00 ]

Absent Instants¶

NaT is ordinary payload for structural assembly. It is neither removed nor expanded and does not prevent neighboring instants from being copied.

Example 5. The absent middle instant retains its exact position.

const auto values = pluss::timeline::make({"2024-01-01", ""});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(
    values.concat(pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-03"))) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[3], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, NaT, 2024-01-03 00:00:00 ]

Failure Modes¶

Validation rejects different ranks after scalar promotion, unequal trailing dimensions, unequal timezone names, an overflowing axis-0 extent, or a total element count that cannot be represented. The vector overload checks every operand before allocating and copying the destination.

Example 6. Trailing-shape, timezone, and rank failures are distinct structural errors.

const std::vector<std::string> values{
    "2024-01-03", "2024-01-04", "2024-01-05"};
try {
  (void)jan12.concat(pluss::timeline::date(values, {3, 1}));
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "rejected\n"; }
try {
  (void)jan12.concat(jan34.tz_convert("America/Edmonton"));
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "rejected\n"; }
try {
  (void)jan12.concat(pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-03"));
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "rejected\n"; }

Output¶

rejected
rejected
rejected
